phase1.intro:
Two workers, same counter, same increment button — and this is where things get genuinely dangerous.

Where should we start?

topics.buttonText: What actually is a race condition?
dialogue: [[key:value++ looks like one instruction, but it's actually three]]: read the current value, add one, write it back. If two threads both read at the same instant, one increment vanishes silently. That's a [[term:race condition]].
[[warn:No exception gets thrown]] — the program runs, prints a number, and that number is simply wrong, and might be wrong only sometimes.

stickyNote.definition: A race condition happens when value++ (read-add-write) overlaps between threads, silently losing an increment — no exception, wrong result.

topics.buttonText: How does synchronized actually fix it?
dialogue: [[term:synchronized]] marks a method or block as something only one thread can be inside at a time. Every object has a built-in lock, and entering synchronized code means acquiring that lock first — any other thread that tries simply waits its turn.

stickyNote.flavor: 🔒 one thread at a time, everyone else waits
stickyNote.definition: synchronized marks a method or block so only one thread can execute it at a time, using the object's built-in lock.

topics.buttonText: When should I synchronize a block instead of the whole method?
dialogue: [[warn:Synchronizing the whole method locks the entire object]], even for code that doesn't need it — a synchronized block, `synchronized(lock) { ... }`, locks only what's inside the braces. [[fun:Static synchronized methods lock on the Class object itself]] instead of an instance.

stickyNote.definition: synchronized on a whole method locks the entire object. synchronized(lock) { ... } locks only that block — usually the finer-grained choice.

mcq.question:
A class has two synchronized instance methods, deposit() and withdraw(), both synchronizing on the same object (the default 'this'). Thread A calls deposit() on accountX while Thread B calls withdraw() on accountY (a DIFFERENT object). What happens?

A) Thread B must wait for Thread A to finish — synchronized always blocks globally
B) Both run concurrently without blocking each other — they're locking different objects' monitors
C) This throws IllegalMonitorStateException
D) Only one Counter object can exist at a time once synchronized is used

phase4.selfChallenge:
Create a BankAccount class with:
• Private balance (double)
• Synchronized deposit(double amount) method
• Synchronized withdraw(double amount) method
• Synchronized getBalance() method

In main:
1. Create a BankAccount with $1000
2. Create 5 threads that each deposit $100 (500 total)
3. Create 3 threads that each withdraw $50 (150 total)
4. All threads run simultaneously
5. Print final balance (should be $1350 if correct)

phase5.trivia: The lock a synchronized method acquires is called the object's "intrinsic lock" or "monitor" — a concept borrowed directly from Tony Hoare's 1974 monitor model for concurrent programming, decades before Java existed.
